A digital angel bridges the hospital bedside gap for mothers of premature newborns.
Evidence: AngelEye cameras, NICU grant, maternal access
#Health #Canberra 🌐

New NICU cameras allow mothers like Erin Thorpe to monitor premature babies remotely via secure app, easing separation anxiety.

Erin Thorpe was shopping for groceries when she felt compelled to rush back to her baby daughter Aubree at Canberra Hospital.

Login or signup to continue reading

"I knew if there was an issue they would call me, but I'd just get this feeling that I had to go back," Mrs Thorpe said.

"I didn't feel like I could leave her bedside or I could leave the hospital."

But with five other children aged between 3 and 11 years at home with her husband Brendan in the Southern Highlands town of Taralga, there are times when Mrs Thorpe simply has to leave the hospital.

Now almost six weeks old, baby Aubree has been a patient in Canberra Hospital's neonatal intensive care unit, after being born prematurely at 30 weeks and 5 days gestation.

Time spent away from Aubree became a little easier for Mrs Thorpe on Thursday 12 November, when an "AngelEye" camera was switched on over the baby's cot.

The video camera allows Mrs Thorpe to see Aubree remotely via a secure app.

When she wakes up during the night to express milk at her Ronald McDonald House accommodation, Mrs Thorpe can reassure herself that Aubree is doing well in the care of the neonatal intensive care nurses.

"I just log on and I just see that she's fine," she said.

Mrs Thorpe was also able to travel home to Taralga for a few hours to attend her 5-old son's kindy orientation.

Aubree is likely to be in Canberra Hospital for several more weeks, before being transferred to Goulburn.

Health Minister Dr Marisa Paterson said the "AngelEyes" had been installed over all 39 beds in the hospital's neonatal intensive care unit and special care nursery.

"This just allows [parents] that opportunity to be able to see their little baby, and also to meet their caring needs or other needs that are required out in the community,'' Dr Paterson said.

The Newborn Intensive Care Foundation funded the installation of the cameras with a $117,000 grant.

Neonatology clinical lead Dr Hazel Carlisle said the cameras were designed especially for hospital wards with babies.
